description: Bongo Aphelion is a Bangladesh-based team participating in NASA Space Apps to explore practical solutions for health monitoring using NASA data and technology. We value hands-on collaboration, problem-solving, and learning. We’re looking for teammates with hackathon experience and skilled in data, AI/ML, design, hardware, or software. Join us to collaborate and build together.
summary: Mission Control Jr. is an interactive 3D browser game where kids (ages 7–12) run outposts on Mars and the Moon. Built with JavaScript, Three.js, and real NASA data, players make critical choices balancing power, water, crops, and radiation shields. Instead of boring quizzes, children see the direct consequences of their decisions. Featuring friendly robot guide Pip, voice narration, and two age levels, it makes genuine space engineering accessible, fun, and inspiring for future explorers.
details:
What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

Mission Control Jr. is a playable, 3D browser-based space training game where children aged 7–12 become junior astronauts managing human outposts on Mars and the Moon.

Rather than passively reading, players explore realistic 3D environments through nine narrative missions and a long-term simulation sandbox.

The core mechanic is the Trade-Off Engine, where players manage limited daily supplies of electricity, oxygen, clean water, and food. Every decision has consequences:

  • Clearing dust from solar panels restores power, but working outside consumes suit battery and oxygen.
  • Powering the greenhouse ensures future food supplies but leaves less energy for water recycling and radiation shields.
  • Emergencies such as dust storms and solar flares require players to prioritize crew safety, repair machinery, and seal airlocks before hazards arrive.

What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Active Cause-and-Effect Learning: Unlike educational apps that rely on multiple-choice quizzes, players learn through immediate, visible consequences. When life support runs low, lights dim and alarms sound. Post-mission reports explain what went wrong and why.
  • Non-Punitive Failure: Mistakes never result in traumatic crew deaths. Instead, unsafe situations trigger a training suspension, followed by friendly debriefings and one-click replays that encourage experimentation and problem-solving.
  • Companion Guidance: A friendly robot named Pip offers advice, helpful tips, and voice read-aloud support, ensuring reading difficulties never prevent children from enjoying space science.

What Is the Intended Impact?

Our goal is to inspire the next generation of space explorers and introduce aerospace engineering to young minds.

By making complex concepts such as closed-loop life support, orbital mechanics, and radiation physics intuitive and engaging, we demonstrate that engineering is not just about formulas. It is also about planning, teamwork, and problem-solving.

We want children from all backgrounds to feel confident that they, too, can explore the cosmos.


What Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software Did We Use?

Frontend & 3D Graphics: Modern JavaScript (ES Modules), HTML5, CSS, and Three.js (WebGL) for real-time 3D rendering.

  • 3D Models & Audio: 19 custom, lightweight procedural 3D models in GLB format, designed for outposts, rovers, and equipment. Bundled crew voice recordings are supported by browser Web Speech API fallbacks.
  • Development & Build Pipeline: Node.js and Vite, with over 240 automated unit tests covering different scenarios.
  • Real NASA Data Integration
  • Hardware Compatibility: Runs entirely in standard desktop browsers without expensive GPUs, downloads, or external cloud servers.

How Is the Project Creative?

  • Living, Dynamic Worlds: Players physically explore Martian terrain, tow solar masts across lunar craters, connect cables, and seal airlocks in real-time 3D rather than simply navigating menus.
  • Realistic Space Communication Delays: Players can radio Earth for assistance when equipment fails, experiencing the actual 14–20-minute one-way communication delay with Mars. They must decide whether to wait for ground control or diagnose problems independently as resources decline.
  • The Pip Companion: A lovable robot that translates complex telemetry into child-friendly explanations, awards badges, and provides cheerful encouragement.

What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

  • Age-Based Difficulty Levels:
    • Cadet (Ages 7–9): Simple language, visual percentage bars, guided waypoints, and forgiving resource limits.
    • Explorer (Ages 10–12): Exact physical units (watts, liters, micrometers), tighter resource limits, and detailed technical telemetry.
  • Inclusion & Accessibility: Full voice-overs, high-contrast text, subtitles, guided navigation controls for players with limited motor control, and a reduced-motion toggle.
  • Low-Resource Environments: A dedicated Low Effects mode ensures smooth performance on affordable school laptops and Chromebooks, including devices with Intel integrated graphics. The game also supports completely offline play after its initial loading.
